rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery elements often outweigh the written joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements like inflection, pace, and rhythm (delivery) are crucial and often more important than the written text of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written word struggles to convey inflection and timing; successful jokes rely heavily on how they are delivered. Emphasize rehearsal and vocal/body techniques to optimize delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: topical jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy material based on current events, cultural trends, fades, and politics usually done on late night talk shows and sketch shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common on one-liners, political humor, and roasts; be mindful of shelf-life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay, puns and apparent misprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning, playful morphological manipulation, and 'misprint'-like constructions are standard technical methods for producing jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include blending words, punning on similar forms, exploiting polysemy, or presenting an apparent typographical error that yields a humorous reinterpretation (e.g., 'Orienterpresszug').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the joke specific (not generic)? / Specificity always.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, particular details rather than generic labels or abstractions; specific images and actions make jokes sharper and funnier. (Example guidance from Fey: to make an audience laugh vs. to make comedy writers laugh—specific staging choices differ.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic ambiguity, puns and linguistic ambiguity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic ambiguity and puns engage specific neural mechanisms linking humour to semantic processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include manipulations of ambiguity (puns vs unambiguous jokes) to probe language-semantic contributions to humour; Bekinschtein et al. show links between humour and semantic ambiguity processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Rules of Humor — Be original
rubrics_metrics.description: Be original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid clichés and predictable angles; originality increases surprise and audience enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfecting delivery via rhythm and musicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Your timing affects how every joke lands; find a rhythm in material like music to know where laughs and pauses belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed over repeated performance. Quote: 'After I do a joke or a bit for a long time, it’s got a rhythm; I know where the laughs are coming or where the pauses are.' Listen for rises in voice and musicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength of the comedy comes from specificity — detailed, concrete images and settings that produce humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review states 'The strength of Torres’ comedy is in his specificity, particularly for the Big Apple’s fluorescent-lit spaces.' Examples include dingy apartments, cracking Ikea furniture, empty Gatorade bottles, and other small details that create comedic gold. Anti-pattern: vague or generic settings that don't yield particular jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline subverts expectation in a connectable way (Is This Funny? rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The punch should overturn the setup in a way the audience can relate to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subversion must be intelligible and resonate with the audience's knowledge or experience to trigger laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context sensitivity and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes gain potency when they engage with the immediate factual and cultural context of a high-profile story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece ties specific jokes to events of the trial (crime-scene tour, acquittal) and subsequent developments (book comments, later arrests for petty theft). Guidance: craft jokes that reference concrete, timely details to increase relevance; anti-pattern: stale or out-of-context references that miss the news cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity, incongruity, and sudden resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jokes involve an interplay of ambiguity, incongruity, and a sudden resolution of that incongruity to elicit laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'two fish in a tank' joke works because ambiguity of the word 'tank' and the incongruity of gun-toting fish produce surprise when the wordplay 'clicks' into place. Computational humor researchers view this ambiguity-incongruity-resolution pattern as a central mechanism for why things are funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to performer and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Different performers and formats require different comedic styles; a dry, conversational joke may 'kill' in a read-through yet be hard to pull off live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smigel contrasts his dry style with performers who 'go small' (Kristen Wiig) and stresses tailoring material to a performer's strengths and the venue. Evaluate whether material fits the performer's instincts and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth (rooted in actual everyday experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth: observational material should be rooted in actual everyday experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground jokes in believable, lived moments; authenticity increases audience buy-in. Avoid fabrications that undermine the feeling of shared reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Anti-Punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Subverting the setup–punchline model by avoiding expected payoffs, ending sketches abruptly, or introducing unrelated elements instead of a conventional conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing Tip: Consider defying comedic conventions by refusing to deliver expected punchlines; sometimes the absence of resolution is funnier. Example Technique: The 'Dead Parrot' sketch extends past a normal payoff into escalating absurd euphemisms, creating humor through repetition rather than a single punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edgy or satirical material should have a point
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'edgy' is not an excuse for thoughtless nastiness — great edgy comedy has a clear satirical point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like South Park: creators make vitriolic observations but always 'know what they're saying.' If performers can't articulate the point, the work likely amounts to relinquishing responsibility rather than satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency subordinated to humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization and consistency could be 'sacrificed to humor'; persona stays where necessary for plot and humor rather than full psychological realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters by their service to comedy and plot rather than by realist consistency. Recurring archetypal behavior is an acceptable and expected technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate escalating hypothetical alternatives for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic internal deliberation listing increasingly absurd or violent options (e.g., considering 'knocking the fellow down and making a bolt'), used to dramatise frustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure thought processes as a sequence of possible responses that escalate from reasonable to absurd; the escalation itself functions as the comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of meanings (word-play and puns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring two independent meanings into the same expression so the sentence supports two sets of ideas simultaneously; the play upon words exploits different meanings (especially figurative vs literal) to reveal a lapse in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns are the crudest form (homophony producing two different sentences); higher forms present one sentence with two legitimate interpretations. The play upon words often feels like a negligence of language and is amusing because it temporarily makes language accommodate things to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness/non-specificity as a comedic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained absence of concrete specifics (objects, issues, people) can itself be the joke and a critique of lazy stand-up styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The set performs for nearly three minutes 'without once mentioning a single object, issue, or human being.' This technique signals the game's premise and can produce strong audience rewards if the crowd recognizes the move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of comedic perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate and include diverse comedic perspectives for each prompt (achieved via multiple personas) to enrich the humor dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity across styles (absurdism, cynicism, etc.) is a criterion for dataset quality — avoid narrow single-style corpora that limit the model's comedic range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific, concrete details chosen to sharpen a joke and make it more vivid/funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description notes 'the phrasing, rhythm, and precise details that make their work so dang funny' — advising careful selection of concrete details to elevate humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual integration / relevance to input
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate original, contextually integrated jokes rather than unrelated or on-request-only jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with conversational AIs that only output jokes written by humans, mostly generate nonsense, only tell jokes on request, or tell jokes unrelated to context. Witscript's aim is to produce jokes integrated with the user's input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of meanings in a sentence (pun vs play on words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises when a single sentence legitimately or seemingly expresses two independent sets of ideas—either via homophony (pun) or via multiple meanings of a word—so the meanings jostle one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pun is a 'less reputable' form (different sentences conflated by sound); more refined play upon words uses one sentence that genuinely accommodates two senses, producing a momentary lapse of language's normal function and hence amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity (Not Generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it specific (not generic)? Specific detail makes jokes more vivid and shareable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, specific images or situations help readers connect and recognize themselves. Avoid vague generalities; specificity often provides the unexpected twist that generates humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that follow too-familiar patterns or lack a surprising twist fail to engage the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to flip everyday situations on their head and think outside expected patterns to preserve surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational — sees the absurd in the ordinary
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational — sees the absurd in the ordinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material should highlight the small absurdities in common experiences. The comedic angle comes from reframing normal situations to reveal their implicit silliness. Avoid abstract or overly theoretical premises that lose the ordinary reference point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic: shared-norms engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the audience shares the norms the joke references or violates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For norm-based humor to work (e.g., mockery, satire), the audience must recognize the relevant norms; effectiveness depends on the degree of shared cultural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and generalizability limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that experimental evaluation focused on one form of humor (standalone jokes/puns), which limits claims about broader humor capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors: 'The present investigation focuses on one specific form of humor, namely standalone jokes.' When evaluating LLM humor, explicitly note which manifestations of humor are covered and avoid overgeneralizing findings to other forms (e.g., situational comedy, satire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual / referential jokes risk limited accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques note the site's material is often 'riffs on riffs, building referential jokes atop the already referential right-wing commentary about the untrustworthiness of the news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy reliance on audience familiarity with specific media narratives or conspiratorial frames can narrow comedic reach and increase chances of misinterpretation by those outside the reference loop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and Personal Expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritizes originality and personal perspective over formulaic jokes—'There are no hacks in alternative comedy... you have to do something original or you're gone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create distinctive material rooted in personal voice and perspective. Avoid relying on comedic 'tricks' or broadly generic setups that sacrifice individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent comic narrator/voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a steady, distinctive narrative voice that delivers humour through ironic, urbane commentary rather than overt explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage uses a gently ironic narrator (e.g., 'Work, the what's-its-name of the thingummy and the thing-um-a-bob of the what d'you-call-it.') who treats absurdity as if it were ordinary, letting the humour arise from tone. Preserve that ironic detachment; avoid switching to straightforward exposition which kills the comic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-Based
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedian performs as a persona or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on sustained persona traits and viewpoints. Examples: Andy Kaufman, Maria Bamford. Useful for exploring perspectives distinct from the performer’s real-life voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected twist / incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it have an unexpected twist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor strongly correlates with incongruity and surprise — an unexpected response or reversal is a core ingredient. Structure the joke so the punchline violates the audience's prediction in a concise way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specificity to make jokes land
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific details make a story unique and help the humor land harder, even when addressing universal experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the Hocus Pocus essay, details like 'Second Empire Victorian built in 1870' or 'Italianate-style cupola' signal a fancy old house and sharpen jokes about repairs. Specificity often improves comedic effect rather than diluting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine clever observation with tightly-wrapped absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'clever observation of the world wrapped up so tightly in absurdity that you almost missed the point while doubled over in hysterics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor surreal elements in a recognisable observation about society or behaviour, then present it through an absurd conceit so the insight is both felt and obscured by the humour. Use of this balance can create moments that are both intellectually satisfying and viscerally funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must understand both possible interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the Three Pillars. The reader needs the background/frames to see the double meaning or ambiguity that the punchline exploits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation: raise stakes and absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: After setup, raise the stakes by making the situation more absurd or challenging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalate conflicts progressively so consequences grow and comedy deepens. Use specific escalating moments that reveal how much worse (and funnier) things can get (example: Liz meets Tracy and discovers he's even crazier than described). Escalation should build toward a midpoint or climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive overload via weakly communicated assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes produce laughter not from a single incongruity-resolution but from a cognitive overload of weakly communicated assumptions: the punchline implies many things simultaneously (about characters, situation, norms, stereotypes) and the proliferation of weak implicatures is itself the source of comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess jokes for the density of weak implicatures: deeper jokes have many resonances; translations often lose force because those assumptions fail to carry; insider jokes are funnier to insiders because more weak assumptions are accessible. For production, design punchlines that trigger a halo of weak implications rather than a single neat reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and precise wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The more specific in comedy the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the most precise, image-creating word possible — brevity and specificity often make a line funnier. For example, a concrete single-word image can out-perform a vague concept. Also consider syllable/word economy for rhythm and punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding and writing for the specific audience who will hear or read the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience is one of the named elements and gets a chapter; the book emphasizes tailoring material to 'whoever they may be' (from wedding guests to viewers of a show).
